alloydb:copy:8: Making ML failures easier to investigate.
alloydb:copy:9: Google Software Engineering Student Program · Building a Python ML workload backed by AlloyDB Omni, with telemetry to connect training failures to database and infrastructure health.
alloydb:copy:29: A failed run should leave a clear trail.
alloydb:copy:31: A failed ML job can stem from model code, compute limits, or storage. Its clues are split across training logs, resource metrics, and database state. We aim to bring that evidence together.
alloydb:copy:33: I coordinate product work and contribute to the Python ML application: reading training data, persisting results in AlloyDB Omni, and integrating with the telemetry team.
alloydb:copy:35: Build the workload. Make it observable.
alloydb:copy:37: Build a Python training workload backed by AlloyDB Omni: a concrete application the team can instrument and diagnose.
alloydb:copy:39: Persist training data and results in a dedicated database. Configure the connection by endpoint so the workload stays independent of deployment location.
alloydb:copy:41: Integrate training logs and metrics through OTLP and shared run identifiers, linking the workload to OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Loki, and Grafana.
alloydb:copy:43: Help an engineer decide what to check next.
alloydb:copy:45: OTel collects application, container, database, host, and GPU signals under shared job/run/rank identifiers. GPU placement and cross-cluster collection remain integration questions.
alloydb:copy:47: Planned: align resource anomalies with logs in a ±30-second window. Triage infrastructure faults (OOM/NCCL), training faults (NaN loss), and persistence faults (connection starvation).
alloydb:copy:49: Planned: unified Grafana views. Stretch: retrieve related incidents and mitigations through AlloyDB Omni pgvector similarity plus PostgreSQL full-text search.
alloydb:copy:51: Show observations before hypotheses: relevant logs and metrics first, then a possible cause and related incidents to investigate.
alloydb:copy:54: In progress: application persistence and telemetry integration. The goal is evidence-based investigation of failed training jobs.
robotic-knitting:copy:8: A more reliable stitch, one coordinated motion at a time.
robotic-knitting:copy:9: Python control and custom tooling for three FAIRINO arms over a 6×6 needle bed. The redesign adds active yarn-tension control during loop transfer.
robotic-knitting:copy:17: Knitting a volume, not just a surface.
robotic-knitting:copy:19: Solid knitting connects loops inside a soft volume, rather than forming only a sheet or shell. Stitch connections build the interior layer by layer.
robotic-knitting:copy:21: Prior work: a 6×6 actuated needle array connected horizontal layers as the form moved downward, producing overhangs and pyramidal forms. Our work builds on that platform.
robotic-knitting:copy:23: Our redesign adds a yarn-distributor arm as a tensioning fixture. Two grippers transfer the stitch while the third secures the yarn.
robotic-knitting:copy:26: The problem, and my part in it.
robotic-knitting:copy:28: Slack during loop transfer can cause missed yarn or inconsistent stitches. A dedicated third arm secures the yarn while two grippers manipulate it.
robotic-knitting:copy:30: I write and debug the motion-control software, test on hardware, and prototype yarn-handling parts in Fusion 360 with Prof. François Guimbretière.
robotic-knitting:copy:34: Map bed coordinates with the FAIRINO Python SDK. Sequence the arms using safe-hover offsets to keep tool paths clear.
robotic-knitting:copy:36: The distributor holds the yarn; the left gripper clears the previous stitch; the right transfers yarn east. The distributor adjusts tension, then releases.
robotic-knitting:copy:38: Servo-driven tools went through repeated physical trials. An inner ridge in the needle helped grippers catch yarn after early failures.
robotic-knitting:copy:42: Give the system a closer view.
robotic-knitting:copy:44: Ongoing: mount cameras on the arms to inspect yarn, tools, and the bed during trials. Use the footage to diagnose failures and decide what to change.
robotic-knitting:copy:45: From a single stitch to a continuous process
robotic-knitting:copy:46: Next: a dedicated tension-adjusting mechanism, continuous operation across the 6×6 bed, and coordination for volumetric knitting. Camera feedback will help diagnose failures as we scale.
robotic-knitting:copy:49: Demonstrated a single actively tensioned stitch. Custom components reduced mechanical failures by 20% against earlier prototypes. Full-bed operation and volumetric knitting are next steps.
